Key Research Thinking Patterns: Behavioral Prezygotic Isolation Assessment: Systematic evaluation of mate choice and conspecific preference to determine the role of behavioral barriers in speciation and hybridization (e.g., Using binary choice tests and Strength of Preference calculations to demonstrate the lack of conspecific preference in Poecilia mexicana and P. latipinna, facilitating the origin of the asexual Amazon molly).

Common Garden Fitness Quantification: Standardized experimental design to isolate genetic effects from environmental plasticity when assessing hybrid viability and life-history trade-offs (e.g., Employing common-garden experiments with controlled light and food conditions to reveal sex-specific dominance patterns and higher mortality in F1 hybrids of cave and surface Poecilia mexicana ecotypes).

Multigenerational Mesocosm Ecology: Long-term maintenance of natural populations in controlled environments to observe the evolutionary consequences of mating systems on non-mating behavioral traits (e.g., Utilizing Brackenridge Field Laboratories mesocosms to link male mating tactics in poeciliid fish to female cognitive flexibility, spatial learning, and movement patterns).

Welfare-Integrated Physiological Monitoring: Integration of environmental enrichment protocols with longitudinal growth and health metrics to optimize animal welfare without compromising experimental validity (e.g., Measuring early-life growth rates and mortality in asexual Amazon molly clones under physical and social enrichment to establish stage-specific welfare benefits).
Summary Description: Ingo Schlupp is an evolutionary biologist specializing in the behavioral ecology and reproductive biology of livebearing fishes (Poeciliidae). His research focuses on the mechanisms of hybrid speciation, reproductive isolation, and the evolutionary impacts of sexual conflict. Utilizing the International Stock Center for Livebearing Fishes, he employs common-garden experiments, multigenerational mesocosms, and rigorous behavioral assays (binary choice, cognitive tasks) to dissect prezygotic and postzygotic isolation in species like the Amazon molly and Atlantic molly. His work bridges fundamental evolutionary questions with applied animal welfare, investigating how environmental enrichment and mating systems influence fitness, cognition, and physiological development. By integrating genetic, ecological, and behavioral data, Schlupp provides critical insights into the origin of new species and the conservation of ecologically distinct fish populations.
